books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, A. Reform Movements in the Antebellum Period

primary_sources: Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843

stimulus.text: "I come to present the strong claims of suffering humanity. . . . I proceed, Gentlemen, briefly to call your attention to the present state of Insane Persons confined within this Commonwealth, in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods, and lashed into obedience!" — Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts (Boston: Munroe & Francis, 1843). Wording checked against the full text at the Disability History Museum and the American Journal of Public Health reprint; ellipses mark omissions.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Dix, Memorial (1843)
stem: Dix's memorial asks the Massachusetts legislature to do which of the following?

options.text: Execute people with mental illness as criminals
options.misconception: Dix wants these people treated as patients, not punished as criminals.

options.text: Send people with mental illness back to their families
options.misconception: Many had no family able to care for them; Dix asks the state to build asylums.
Dix wants more asylums built, not fewer.

options.text: Build separate, humane asylums for people with mental illness

rationales.A: Dix calls the confined 'suffering humanity' and asks for relief, not punishment. Execution is the opposite of her plea.
rationales.B: Dix's cases show people locked in almshouses and jails, not cared for at home. Her answer is state asylums, not family care.
rationales.C: Dix's memorial led to the expansion of the Worcester asylum. She wanted the state to build asylums, not close them.
rationales.D: Dix shows the insane kept in cages and stalls, then asks the legislature to give them proper asylums. Her plea is for humane, separate care.
rationales.general:
1. Hear the plea. Dix calls herself the advocate of helpless, forgotten people.
2. See the evidence. She lists cages, closets, cellars, stalls, and pens.
3. Name the ask. She wants the state to build asylums where these people are treated as patients.
Background: Dix visited jails and almshouses across Massachusetts in 1840 and 1841 before writing the memorial.
Remember: a reformer's evidence points at her remedy — the horror she lists is the thing her remedy replaces.
